title: Pressure-cooker gammon joint
subtitle: Tender, sliceable gammon in 45 minutes
excerpt: A whole gammon joint cooked under pressure in stock and aromatics until it yields in clean, glossy slices. A Christmas and Sunday dinner staple that normally takes hours, ready in under an hour.
sourceNotes: Gammon is a British cured ham joint. Boiling or braising gammon is traditional, the long cook removes excess salt while tenderising the meat. The pressure cooker compresses the usual 2 to 3 hours to about 45 minutes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice after cooking and freeze in airtight portions for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook and refrigerate the joint whole. Slice cold, it holds together better. Serve at room temperature or reheat in the glaze under the grill.

content.text: Gammon is cured pork and needs a long cook to tenderise the meat and draw out some of the salt. In a saucepan, this takes 20 minutes per 500 g, a 1.5 kg joint requires over an hour. The pressure cooker cuts this to 45 minutes while producing juicier, evenly cooked meat because the moisture cannot escape.

If the gammon has been soaked overnight in cold water, it will be less salty. If not, the pressure-cooking liquid will remove much of the excess salt anyway, use plain water rather than stock so the finished cooking liquid is not too salty to discard.

The optional glaze and grill step after cooking gives the joint a caramelised exterior. It is not required, the gammon is fully cooked from the pot, but it makes the presentation significantly better and adds flavour.

Put the gammon joint in the pressure cooker. Add the onion, carrot, celery, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Cover with cold water, the joint should be fully submerged. Do not add salt. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 45 minutes for a 1.5 kg joint. Add 5 minutes per extra 500 g. Allow a natural pressure release of 15 minutes, then quick-release the rest.

Lift the gammon out and peel off the rind, leaving the fat layer intact. Score the fat in a diamond pattern with a sharp knife. Mix the honey and mustard together and brush over the fat. Transfer to a foil-lined roasting tin and place under a hot grill for 5 to 8 minutes until the glaze is caramelised and catching at the edges. Rest for 15 minutes before carving.

rows.symptom: The gammon is still tough in the centre
rows.cause: The joint was denser than expected, or pressure was not maintained throughout.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 15 minutes. When a skewer meets no resistance in the thickest part, it is done.

rows.cause: The joint was not soaked before cooking, and the cooking water retained the salt.
rows.fix: Soak the joint in cold water overnight before cooking next time. Also discard the cooking liquid rather than using it as stock.

rows.symptom: The glaze burns before it sets
rows.cause: The grill was too close, or the honey content was very high.
rows.fix: Move the tin down a level in the oven and watch closely, the glaze caramelises quickly and can go from golden to burnt in under a minute.

content.text: Gammon is a British Sunday and Christmas centrepiece, presented whole, carved at the table, and accompanied by parsley sauce, mash, or roasted root vegetables. Leftovers are arguably the best part: cold gammon in sandwiches with mustard, or diced into a split pea soup. The pressure cooker version makes a weeknight gammon viable and produces a Sunday joint without the three-hour wait.
